items.title: Seven Stages of Attention That Carry a Mind from Ordinary Distraction into Absorption

items.zh: 於有漏方便中，先說解脫，後說三摩地。由證方便究竟作意果煩惱斷已，方得根本三摩地故。或有俱時說三摩地及與解脫。謂即於此方便究竟作意及餘無間道三摩地中，由三摩地與彼解脫俱時有故。
items.en: Within the contaminated method, liberation is taught first and concentration second — because it is only once the culminating attention that perfects this method has severed affliction that the fundamental concentration itself is actually attained.

items.title: The Five Hindrances Begin: Desire, and the Prince Who Reasoned His Way Past It

items.zh: 復次，於諸靜慮、等至障中，略有五蓋，將證彼時能為障礙。何等為五？一、貪欲蓋，二、瞋恚蓋，三、惛沈睡眠蓋，四、掉舉惡作蓋，五、疑蓋。
items.en: Further, among the obstructions to the meditative absorptions and attainments, there are, briefly, five hindrances, capable of obstructing their realisation. What are the five? First, the hindrance of desire. Second, the hindrance of ill will. Third, the hindrance of dullness and drowsiness. Fourth, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse. Fifth, the hindrance of doubt.

items.zh: 貪欲者，謂於妙五欲隨逐淨相，欲見、欲聞，乃至欲觸；或隨憶念先所領受，尋伺追戀。
items.en: Desire is this: chasing after the appealing appearance of attractive sensory objects, wishing to see, to hear, and so on through to wishing to touch them; or, recalling what has been enjoyed before, dwelling on it with coarse and subtle thought, longing after it still.

items.title: Ill Will, and the Seven Ordinary Causes of Dullness and Drowsiness

items.zh: 瞋恚者，謂或因同梵行等舉其所犯，或因憶念昔所曾經不饒益事瞋恚之相，心生恚怒；或欲當作不饒益事，於當所為瞋恚之相多隨尋伺，心生恚怒。
items.en: Ill will is this: whether from a fellow practitioner pointing out one's own fault, or from recalling some past harm and its accompanying resentment, anger arises; or, intending some future harm to another, dwelling repeatedly on that resentment with coarse and subtle thought, anger arises.

items.zh: 惛沈者，謂或因毀壞淨尸羅等隨一善行、不守根門、食不知量、不勤精進減省睡眠、不正知住而有所作、於所修斷不勤加行，隨順生起一切煩惱，身心惛昧，無堪任性。睡眠者，謂心極昧略。又順生煩惱、壞斷加行，是惛沈性；心極昧略，是睡眠性。是故此二、合說一蓋。
items.en: Dullness is this: from breaking pure moral discipline or any other wholesome practice, from failing to guard the sense-doors, from not knowing moderation in eating, from lacking the diligence to reduce sleep, from acting without clear awareness of what one is doing, or from failing to apply effort to what should be cultivated and abandoned, or from going along with the arising of any affliction — body and mind grow dull and clouded, unfit for the task. Drowsiness is this: the mind utterly dimmed and drawn in. This is why the two are spoken of together as a single hindrance.

items.zh: 又惛昧無堪任性、名惛沈；惛昧心極略性，名睡眠。由此惛沈生諸煩惱、隨煩惱時，無餘近緣如睡眠者。諸餘煩惱及隨煩惱或應可生，或應不生。若生惛昧，睡眠必定皆起。掉舉者，謂因親屬尋思、國土尋思、不死尋思，或隨憶念昔所經歷戲笑歡娛所行之事，心生諠動騰躍之性。

items.title: Remorse Over Leaving Home, and a Bodhisattva's Poem to a Homesick Boy

items.zh: 惡作者，謂因尋思親屬等故，心生追悔，謂我何緣離別親屬？何緣不往如是國土？何緣棄捨如是國土，來到於此，食如是食，飲如是飲，唯得如是衣服、臥具、病緣醫藥資身眾具？我本何緣少小出家，何不且待至年衰老？或因追念昔所曾經戲笑等事，便生悔恨，謂我何緣於應受用戲樂、嚴具、朋遊等時，違背宗親朋友等意，令其悲戀涕淚盈目而強出家。
items.en: Remorse is this: dwelling on thoughts of family and the rest, regret arises — why did I leave my family behind? Why did I not go to such-and-such a place instead? ... Why did I renounce the world so young, rather than waiting until old age? Or, recalling past amusements once enjoyed, regret arises — why, at a time I should have been enjoying entertainment, fine adornment, and the company of friends, did I instead go against the wishes of my family and companions, leaving them grieving and in tears, and insist on renouncing the world regardless?

items.zh: 由如是等種種因緣，生憂戀心，惡作追悔。由前掉舉與此惡作處所等故，合說一蓋。又於應作、不應作事，隨其所應，或已曾作、或未曾作，心生追悔。云何我昔應作不作，非作反作。除先追悔所生惡作，此惡作纏、猶未能捨。次後復生相續不斷憂戀之心，惡作追悔。此又一種惡作差別。次前所生非處惡作及後惡作、雖與掉舉處所不等，然如彼相，騰躍諠動，今此亦是憂戀之相，是故與彼雜說一蓋。
疑者：謂於師、於法、於學、於誨，及於證中生惑生疑。由心如是懷疑惑故，不能趣入勇猛方便，正斷寂靜。又於去來今及苦等諦生惑生疑，心懷二分、迷之不了，猶豫猜度。問：
items.en: Doubt is this: uncertainty and confusion arising towards one's teacher, the teaching, the trainings, the instructions given, or towards realisation itself — and because the mind is caught in such doubt, it cannot enter courageously into diligent effort, or realise the peace of genuine cessation. Further, uncertainty and confusion arise towards the past, future, and present, and towards the truth of suffering and the rest — the mind torn between two possibilities, unable to resolve the confusion, wavering and merely guessing.

blocks.text: Today's reading introduces the **five hindrances** (五蓋), the classical list of obstacles every meditator meets: sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. The treatise describes how each arises in practice, with examples. Recognising them by name is half the work of overcoming them.

The treatise outlines how attention carries a mind from ordinary distraction into absorption, in seven stages, which fascicle 11 will explain at length. Venerable Miào Jìng adds a point on honesty: a practitioner of worldly dhyāna knows by investigative attention that subtle desire is still present. The seeds are not yet destroyed, and seeing this avoids overestimation (Day 66).

The first hindrance, **sensual desire** (貪欲蓋), is illustrated by a Jātaka. Master Cháng Bǎi: in a former life the Buddha was a king with no son, who asked Śakra for one; the story shows desire reasoned away by seeing its consequences.

subs.head: Ill will, and dullness and drowsiness

blocks.text: **Ill will** (瞋恚蓋) arises from dwelling on wrongs done to oneself or those one loves. **Dullness and drowsiness** (惛沈睡眠蓋) have seven ordinary causes, among them not guarding the senses and overeating. Venerable Miào Jìng on the first: "Always grasping outward tires the spirit; a tired spirit nods off; that's really how it is." Restraint of the senses is not only ethics; it is energy management for meditation.

**Restlessness** (掉舉) is the mind's agitation; **remorse** (惡作) is regret. The treatise gives an example of regret over having left home: "Why did I renounce so young, rather than waiting until old age?" Venerable Miào Jìng: this is "thinking one won't die", assuming there is plenty of time. A bodhisattva's poem to a homesick young monk follows; its consolation is the shortness of life.

**Doubt** (疑蓋) can concern the teacher, the teaching, the training, the instruction, or realisation. Venerable Miào Jìng: "Of these, I think doubting the teacher is gravest; doubting the teacher, you can't follow his teaching."

In practice, the value of the five hindrances is diagnostic. When sitting goes badly, name the hindrance: craving for something, aversion to something, dullness, agitation or regret, or doubt. Each has a different remedy, which tomorrow's and the following readings describe: what "feeds" each hindrance and what "starves" it. Naming comes first; you cannot starve what you have not recognised.

quiz.q: Why does mindfulness-foundation practice need concentration first, per Venerable Miào Jìng?
options: without concentration the mind is scattered, and mindfulness practice lacks the strength to cut afflictions
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "Without concentration your mind is scattered; practising the four foundations won't work — it can't cut afflictions; the strength isn't there." He adds that when calm is overrun by thoughts, one may switch to insight — alternating the two.

quiz.q: How does a practitioner of worldly dhyāna know they haven't fully cut desire, per Venerable Miào Jìng?
options: through investigative attention — one sees subtle desire still present, avoiding overestimation
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "One knows for oneself it isn't fully cut — subtle desire is still there"; "the seeds aren't destroyed for good; they remain, so one is still ordinary." This is the attention of investigation among the seven.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what are the five hindrances?
options: desire, ill will, dullness-drowsiness, restlessness-remorse, doubt
quiz.why: "First, the hindrance of desire. Second, … ill will. Third, … dullness and drowsiness. Fourth, … restlessness and remorse. Fifth, … doubt." They obstruct realising the absorptions. Venerable Miào Jìng: the "obstruction" is affliction itself.

quiz.q: One cause of dullness is not guarding the senses. Why does outward grasping cause dullness, per Venerable Miào Jìng?
options: constantly grasping outward wears out the spirit, and a worn-out spirit dozes
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "Always grasping outward tires the spirit; a tired spirit nods off — that's really how it is." The text lists breaking precepts, unguarded senses, immoderate eating, not reducing sleep, acting without awareness, and slack effort.

quiz.q: Remorse includes "Why did I renounce so young, rather than waiting until old?" Which kind of thought is this, per Venerable Miào Jìng?
options: thoughts of not dying — assuming there's plenty of time
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "'Why not wait until old age to renounce? Wouldn't that be nice? Why so early?' — this is thinking one won't die." §16 lists such thoughts as food for restlessness and remorse.

quiz.q: Doubt can concern teacher, teaching, training, instruction, or realisation. Which does Venerable Miào Jìng consider gravest?
options: doubting the teacher — then one can't follow his instruction
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "Of these, I think doubting the teacher is gravest — doubting the teacher, you can't follow his teaching." He adds that "realising peaceful cessation" is the truth of cessation, "courageous effort" the path.
